<reason>Both sides built coherent frameworks, but B's case was anchored more effectively in concrete mechanisms (Terra's run, USDC's SVB exposure) that A struggled to fully neutralize—A's response that "exposure doesn't establish supervising the issuer resolves the problem" left the SVB point more asserted than answered. The decisive moment came when B extracted A's own limiting principle (bank/MMF treatment triggers when the issuer invests backing assets) and showed that, by A's own test, every major real-world issuer already crosses that line, making the "software-default" category empty in practice. A's closing conceded this convergence for existing issuers and retreated to a purely prospective argument about incentivizing future safer architectures—a real point, but one that effectively surrenders the practical stakes of the motion as it applies to actual stablecoins today. A did land a clean grounding win by catching B's overstated "Tether collapse" claim in pressure questions, and B's clipped opening is a genuine execution cost, but these did not offset B's stronger evidentiary use and the more damaging final exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing (turn 9) applying A's own stated limiting principle ("invests customer backing assets") to real issuers like Circle and Tether, forcing A's closing (turn 10) into a concession that under A's own framework, all current major issuers would already receive bank/MMF-style treatment.</best_rebuttal>
